title: Prom

jokes.text: I can't hear! And I'm dying!
jokes.setup: Ben is surprised by a loud noise/gesture from Leslie trying to be romantic
jokes.punchline: Ben's panicked, hyperbolic reaction — 'I can't hear! And I'm dying!' — to what turns out to be a sweet proposal
jokes.explanation: Quick physical comedy beat that opens the episode. Ben's dramatic overreaction is consistent with his anxious personality. The economy is excellent — two short sentences do a lot of work establishing the comedic tone. Not groundbreaking but a clean opener.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I have a surprise for you!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God, oh my God, oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is the most incredible thing that has ever happened in the history of surprises and cake and life itself!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's just a cupcake.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A CUPCAKE?! This changes everything!

jokes.text: Well, this just keeps getting weirder.
jokes.setup: Ben opens a drawer to find a cake with a prom proposal written on it
jokes.punchline: His dry, resigned commentary on the escalating strangeness of Leslie's romantic gesture
jokes.explanation: Clean deadpan from Ben. The line lands because it acknowledges the absurdity of the situation (loud surprise + cake proposal) without over-explaining it. Ben's straight-man quality is well-deployed here.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my god, is this... is this a promposal?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's a cake. Someone put a message in a cake.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, this is the most romantic thing that's ever happened to me.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We're in our thirties. We've been married for five years.

jokes.text: Plus, I made out with Harvey from the A.V. Club. Hmm, I think I'm jealous of Harvey. You shouldn't be. A few weeks later, he almost died from a VCR electrocution.
jokes.setup: Leslie mentions making out with Harvey; Ben playfully admits jealousy, implying concern about her romantic past
jokes.punchline: Leslie deflects the jealousy not by reassuring Ben emotionally but by telling him Harvey almost died — completely sidestepping the romantic dimension
jokes.explanation: A nicely structured exchange. Ben's 'I think I'm jealous of Harvey' is a sweet, relatable beat, and the pivot to VCR electrocution is unexpected and specific. The specificity (VCR, not just 'electronics') is what elevates it from a generic misdirection joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to teach A.P. Latin at the high school. I've already started preparing. Well, I've started preparing to prepare.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to be honest with you, I don't actually know Latin yet. But I'm a quick learner, and I have a lot of enthusiasm, which is basically the same thing.

jokes.text: Legend has it that he can still turn on a microwave just by blinking at it.
jokes.setup: Leslie describes Harvey's near-fatal VCR electrocution
jokes.punchline: She escalates to a completely absurd folk legend about Harvey having gained microwave-activation superpowers
jokes.explanation: The absurdist escalation here is genuinely delightful. 'Legend has it' gives it a mythological weight that makes the mundane punchline (microwave-blinking) funnier. This is classic Leslie world-building — she treats a trivial high school story with the gravity of ancient lore. Highly quotable in the right crowd.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So Harvey was electrocuted by a VCR and now he has superhero powers?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's not how electricity works.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, it happened to Spider-Man.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Spider-Man was bitten by a radioactive spider.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Same thing.

jokes.text: Well, I thought you'd never ask, because we're nearing 40.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Ben to go to prom with her
jokes.punchline: Ben accepts but undercuts the romance by noting they're nearly 40 — adults going to a teen prom
jokes.explanation: Serviceable joke that acknowledges the premise's inherent absurdity. Economy is strong but the observation itself isn't particularly original — the 'adults doing teen things' joke writes itself.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, will you go to prom with me?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, we're in our thirties.

jokes.text: Aw, did you want to DJ, little puppy? I didn't know that little puppies could operate an iPod with their little puppy paws.
jokes.setup: Ben expresses interest in DJing the prom
jokes.punchline: Tom condescendingly baby-talks Ben as if he were a confused puppy, mocking his presumption about music taste
jokes.explanation: Very Tom Haverford. The baby-talk condescension is a great character move — Tom sees himself as a tastemaker and Ben as hopelessly uncool. 'Little puppy paws' is a funny image. The repetition of 'little puppy' lands because Tom commits to the bit.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, did somebody need help with the music? Is the big strong Ben having trouble with the complicated DJ equipment? Does Ben need Tom to help him? Yes he does! Yes he does!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Tom, I'm literally standing right here.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, is somebody upset? Is Benjamin having a sad? Do we need a juice box and a nap-nap time?

jokes.text: I did DJ a little back in the day. I had a show called 'Zoot Suit Wyatt' on Carleton College radio. Tuesdays from 3:00 to 5:00 A.M., I was the king of swing.
jokes.setup: Ben defends his DJ credentials
jokes.punchline: His credentials are a college radio show called 'Zoot Suit Wyatt' airing at 3 AM — the specificity of the failure is the joke
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. 'Zoot Suit Wyatt' as a DJ name for a nerdy government accountant is deeply funny, and 'Tuesdays from 3:00 to 5:00 A.M.' confirms it was a dead-air show nobody listened to while he called himself 'king of swing.' The specificity (Carleton College, the exact time slot) is what makes this a great joke rather than a generic 'nerdy past' reveal. Rewatch bonus because you can picture exactly who Ben was in college.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I hate both of you so much right now.

jokes.text: I thought we as a culture agreed to forget the year that everyone was into swing.
jokes.setup: Ben proudly announces he was 'king of swing'
jokes.punchline: Tom invokes a collective cultural agreement to erase that embarrassing era
jokes.explanation: Sharp cultural observation. The framing of 'we as a culture agreed' gives this a mock-legislative authority that's very Tom. It's both a burn on Ben and a genuinely relatable cultural reference. Punchy and well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I used to DJ.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Really? That's so cool! What was your DJ name?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: DJ Lord Nightosphere.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my god.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I played weddings... from 2 to 4 AM.

jokes.text: Are those jense-trodder color tabs? I thought those were discontinued. They were. I had to order them through some Mexican back channels. Juan Julio Oficina Supplies? I thought they went out of business. They did, but they opened up a new one in Oaxaca.
jokes.setup: Allison presents a binder with elaborate organizational tabs; Ron inspects it
jokes.punchline: Ron and Allison bond intensely over obscure discontinued office supply brands and black-market procurement networks — treating mundane stationery like contraband
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. Ron Swanson's passionate connoisseurship of quality goods is a core character trait, and having him immediately recognize and rhapsodize over discontinued binder tabs establishes an instant kinship with Allison — while being completely absurd to everyone else ('What is happening right now?'). 'Mexican back channels' for office supplies is a perfect escalation. The Oaxaca detail is the cherry on top. The joke works on multiple levels: Ron's character, the absurdity of treating stationery like contraband, and the comic juxtaposition of Leslie watching her mentorship candidate get stolen by Ron over binder tabs.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Swing music is back, baby. And you know what that means? White people are gonna ruin it again. They already did it once in the '40s, now they're doing it again. Pretty soon every coffee shop in Brooklyn is gonna have a swing band, and they're all gonna be named things like 'The Ironic Nostalgia' or 'Suspenders.'

jokes.text: What is happening right now?
jokes.setup: Ron and Allison have gone deep into a niche conversation about discontinued binder tab brands
jokes.punchline: Leslie's bewildered interjection as the straight man watching this unfold
jokes.explanation: A solid reaction beat that punctuates joke #10. It's the standard sitcom 'voice of the audience' move, and it works, but it's functional rather than brilliant.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, that binder organization is incredible. What tabs are those?

dialogue.speaker: Allison
dialogue.line: Reinforced Acco brand, 1.5 inch, obtained from the office supply distributor in Des Moines.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: How do you know so much about office supplies?

dialogue.speaker: Allison
dialogue.line: I subscribe to three different office supply catalogs. I also have a contact at a paper distributor in Portland who alerts me to new stock arrivals.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's... that's very thorough.

dialogue.speaker: Allison
dialogue.line: I also have a man in Düsseldorf who sources German-engineered ergonomic desk organizers. They're not available in the United States, but I get them imported quarterly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You have an international office supply connection?

dialogue.speaker: Allison
dialogue.line: Several, actually. There's a filing cabinet manufacturer in Milan I work with closely.

jokes.text: Every song I download has to pass a series of rigorous tests to answer one simple question: Is it a banger? How many beats per minute? How many drops? How dope are the drops? Were any acoustic instruments used? If so, it is not a banger.
jokes.setup: Ben suggests they make a set list
jokes.punchline: Tom reveals his pseudo-scientific 'banger test' methodology, which is simultaneously ridiculous and perfectly logical for his character
jokes.explanation: Classic Tom Haverford. His music snobbery rendered as a corporate quality-control process is perfectly absurd. The escalating specificity ('How many drops? How dope are the drops?') builds nicely, and the acoustic instrument disqualifier is a strong punchline. This is Tom at his most Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Why are you two talking about staplers like you just discovered fire?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, you wouldn't understand. Allison gets it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Gets what? That Swingline makes a good stapler?

dialogue.speaker: Allison
dialogue.line: See, he doesn't get it.

jokes.text: I once accidentally downloaded a Lumineers song. I had to throw away my whole computer just to be safe.
jokes.setup: Tom explains his rigorous anti-acoustic instrument policy
jokes.punchline: He escalates the consequence of a Lumineers download to computer destruction — treating musical contamination like a virus requiring hardware disposal
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's sharpest standalone joke. The Lumineers are a perfect specific target — folksy indie rock that's the polar opposite of Tom's EDM/hip-hop taste. The escalation to 'I had to throw away my whole computer just to be safe' is perfectly calibrated: the logic is internally consistent (digital contamination requires hardware disposal) while being completely absurd. The delivery would land as a near-perfect deadpan. Highly quotable. Strong rewatch bonus because the specificity of the Lumineers makes it funnier each time.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I have a very scientific approach to determining if a song bangs. First, I check the bass frequency at the drop. Then I calculate the BPM relative to the optimal dance tempo. I cross-reference the artist's previous chart performance with current streaming algorithms. Finally, I consult my spreadsheet.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: If all metrics align, then yes, the song bangs. If not, it does not bang.

jokes.text: I mean, we're basically vibe curators.
jokes.setup: Ben tries to engage with Tom's DJ philosophy on equal footing
jokes.punchline: Ben using the phrase 'vibe curators' — corporate/millennial language that reveals he thinks he's being cool while confirming he is not
jokes.explanation: A nice character moment showing Ben trying and failing to speak Tom's language. The cringe of 'vibe curators' landing with earnest pride is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, no, no. A banger has to have a drop. It has to have a build-up. You can't just have a guy with an acoustic guitar singing about his feelings.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, what is this? Oh my God. Oh my God, no. No, no, no!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I accidentally downloaded an acoustic version of 'Treat Yo Self.' I need to go to the hospital. I think I'm having a stroke.

jokes.text: I hope that high school auditorium's big enough, 'cause I'm bringing 10,000 maniacs.
jokes.setup: Ben and Tom are discussing what music to play
jokes.punchline: Ben uses '10,000 Maniacs' (the 90s band) as a pun, meaning both the literal band and a crowd of maniacs — which is also completely uncool by Tom's standards
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed pun that works on two levels: it's both a terrible DJ song choice (reinforcing Ben's uncoolness) and a decent wordplay joke. The double meaning is clean and doesn't need explaining. Ben's delivery of this as if it's clever while Tom reacts with horror makes it land as character comedy too.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You know, a good DJ set is all about flow and pacing. You build momentum, take people on a journey.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I was looking at my playlist and I've got 10,000 Maniacs on there.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: At this point, I'd say I've got 10,000 Maniacs and exactly zero chill.

jokes.text: Sometimes it's really hard to be friends with you. Thank God we don't have to be seen together. Yes, we do. We're co-DJs. Not anymore.
jokes.setup: Tom laments how hard it is to be friends with Ben after the pun
jokes.punchline: Tom announces they won't be seen together, Ben points out they're co-DJs — leading to Tom's 'Not anymore,' setting up the DJ Robo Drop reveal
jokes.explanation: Functional bridge joke leading to the DJ Robo Drop reveal. The dynamic between Tom and Ben is well-established; this is more setup than payoff but earns a chuckle.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I guess you could say that joke was... a real hit!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ben, that was the worst thing I've ever heard, and I once listened to Treat Yo Self: The Musical.

jokes.text: DJ Robo Drop reveals himself — a robot DJ costume
jokes.setup: Tom announces he's replacing Ben as co-DJ
jokes.punchline: Tom reveals he has a full DJ robot costume/persona called 'DJ Robo Drop,' which is absurd overkill for a high school prom
jokes.explanation: Tom prepared an elaborate DJ alter-ego with a robot costume for a free high school prom. This is perfect Tom — the effort-to-occasion mismatch is enormous. The musical sting (ba-da-da mm mm mm) implies a full theatrical reveal. Rewatch bonus for the visual.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm DJ Roomba. Whirrrr whirrrr whirrrr.

jokes.text: Oh, I hope that this prom is exactly like my senior prom. Theme: 'My heart will go on.' Photo booth with Monica Lewinsky look-alike. After-party -- Megan Rickerson's house. Her parents used to let us drink as much as we wanted. That's where we should have this after-party. Or, no, we can't, because they moved to prison.
jokes.setup: Tom nostalgically describes his ideal prom based on his senior experience
jokes.punchline: The escalating absurdity peaks with 'they moved to prison' as the reason the after-party venue is unavailable
jokes.explanation: Each detail escalates nicely: Titanic theme → Monica Lewinsky look-alike → parents who let teens drink → 'they moved to prison.' The casual delivery of 'they moved to prison' as if it's merely a logistical problem rather than a significant life development is what makes it land. The Lewinsky detail is funny on its own as a period-specific absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: My parents were so cool. They'd let us drink at after-parties.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: They're in prison now.

jokes.text: Prom is nothing but a huge party full of smiling, dancing people enjoying themselves. It's literally my worst nightmare. And I hate punch.
jokes.setup: April describes prom in a talking head
jokes.punchline: April's definition of her 'worst nightmare' is simply people being happy, then she adds 'And I hate punch' as a coda — the specificity of hating punch is funnier than any dramatic statement
jokes.explanation: This is quintessential April Ludgate. 'It's literally my worst nightmare' is expected from her, but then 'And I hate punch' — delivered as an afterthought with equal weight — is the perfect button. The mundane specificity of hating punch after describing a nightmare scenario is exactly how April's brain works. The structure (dramatic statement + absurd coda) is clean and the character integration is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Prom is this weird thing where they try to make high school fun by decorating the gym and playing music and having a dance. But it's actually just a nightmare where you have to wear an uncomfortable dress and dance with someone you don't like while your parents take pictures.

jokes.text: April Ludgate, I'm gonna sing to you a song that I first wrote 15 years ago for my prom date, Sarah Weiss.
jokes.setup: Andy is about to ask April to prom romantically
jokes.punchline: He reveals the song he's going to sing is a recycled 15-year-old song written for a completely different girl — and names her
jokes.explanation: Andy's complete lack of romantic guile — announcing upfront that this is a repurposed love song for someone else — is perfectly in character. The naming of 'Sarah Weiss' is a nice specific touch. Sets up the song bit well.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Prom is my nightmare. Everyone's sweaty, the music is loud, and worst of all, they never fill the punch bowl more than halfway. It's disrespectful to the punch.

jokes.text: ♪ You're as hot as the sun / But you're as cold as ice / Let me take you to paradise / Come on, roll the dice / It will be twice as nice / Sarah Wei-- April Ludgate ♪
jokes.setup: Andy sings his 'romantic' song for April, which we know was written for Sarah Weiss
jokes.punchline: The song is deliberately terrible (rhymes are forced, lyrics are generic), culminating in Andy starting to sing 'Sarah Wei--' before catching himself and correcting to 'April Ludgate'
jokes.explanation: The payoff works on two levels: the song itself is hilariously bad (paradise/dice/twice as nice forced rhymes), and the inevitable slip to 'Sarah Wei--' lands the callback with perfect timing. Andy not only fails to disguise the recycled nature of the song but almost sings the wrong name at the climactic moment. The correction to 'April Ludgate' — full name, not 'April' — is a nice absurd touch. Strong rewatch bonus because you can see it coming and it still delivers.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: ♪ Ann, Ann, Ann... uh, April, April, April ♪

jokes.text: Fine. I'll go with you, because Leslie's making us, and we live together, and we only have one car right now because you laked mine.
jokes.setup: Andy asks if April will go to prom after his song
jokes.punchline: April's acceptance is framed entirely as logistical obligation, then introduces the mysterious word 'laked'
jokes.explanation: April's anti-romantic acceptance is perfectly in character. But the real gem here is 'laked' — a made-up past-tense verb that sets up a great follow-up beat.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, will you go to prom with me?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Fine. You've laked me into it.

jokes.text: What does 'laked' mean? I tried to jump it over a lake.
jokes.setup: April uses the word 'laked' as if it's perfectly normal
jokes.punchline: April explains that 'laked' means she tried to jump the car over a lake — the casual explanation of an insane act is funnier than any dramatic reveal
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. The construction is nearly perfect: the invented verb 'laked' is a completely natural-sounding word, Larry asks the obvious question, and April's deadpan explanation ('I tried to jump it over a lake') is maximally absurd while being delivered as pure fact. The economy is exceptional — four words to explain an insane event. It's also perfectly April: she destroyed a car attempting something fundamentally stupid and reports it with zero remorse or drama. Then the bonus punchline of 'Why don't you stay out of our conversations, Larry!' makes it even better. Highly quotable, iconic April moment.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What does 'laked' mean?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You drove your car into a lake.

jokes.text: Why don't you stay out of our conversations, Larry!
jokes.setup: Larry asked a perfectly reasonable question ('What does laked mean?') and got a perfectly reasonable answer
jokes.punchline: April snaps at Larry for 'intruding' on a conversation he had every right to join, reinforcing the running Larry-dismissal gag
jokes.explanation: The Larry dismissal is a running gag in Parks and Rec that works here because it's doubly absurd — he asked a question directly relevant to the conversation and got chastised for it. The joke is partly in the injustice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We have a new internship program. I've named it the Thomas Jefferson Memorial WistfulGgs Cavity Meditative Yoga Breath Work Internship Program for Promising Young Adults.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I named it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to rename it tomorrow.

jokes.text: We here at the parks department have something called 'The April Ludgate Summer Solstice Druid Festival and Buffalo Wings Eating Contest.' I don't know why I let her name it.
jokes.setup: Leslie describes the parks department's summer internship program to Allison
jokes.punchline: The program has been renamed by April to a gloriously absurd title, and Leslie's footnote ('I don't know why I let her name it') is understated resignation
jokes.explanation: The full name is absurdist and perfectly April (druid festival + buffalo wings eating contest), and Leslie's admission that she allowed this naming reveals the warm chaos of their relationship. 'I don't know why I let her name it' lands as the punchline because it implies Leslie absolutely does know why — April bullied her into it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait. You two know each other? From where?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: We met at a woodworking conference in 1987.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A woodworking conference? Ron, that's exactly the kind of place where the shadow government would recruit people. Think about it. Wood is a natural material. Nature is controlled by the Illuminati.

dialogue.speaker: Allison
dialogue.line: That doesn't make any sense.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Doesn't it? Or does it make TOO much sense? You were both there. You both work in government. You both have excellent posture. Allison, you have excellent taste in scarves. Ron, you have excellent taste in breakfast meats. What if the conference wasn't about woodworking at all? What if it was about identifying people of exceptional quality and recruiting them into a secret society dedicated to excellence?

jokes.text: Is there some secret society for the greatest humans on earth? Do you meet Tom Hanks and Elena Kagan in the Statue of Liberty's crown?
jokes.setup: Ron and Allison discover they already know each other through Allison's father's hardware store
jokes.punchline: Leslie invents an elaborate fantasy society of great humans meeting in the Statue of Liberty's crown, rattling off Tom Hanks and Elena Kagan as members — revealing her hero worship and fan-fiction brain
jokes.explanation: Very Leslie. The specific pairing of Tom Hanks (beloved actor) and Elena Kagan (Supreme Court Justice) is both unexpected and exactly right for Leslie's pantheon of heroes. The Statue of Liberty's crown as meeting venue is inspired. This joke reveals Leslie's character through a single improvised fantasy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've mapped out a detailed conspiracy involving the city council, a secret tunneling operation, and why Ben keeps disappearing on Thursdays.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait... I just realized I invented all of this in my head while looking at a city planning document and Ben's calendar.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm basically just a very enthusiastic person with a binder and a problem.

jokes.text: God, this fake club I'm inventing is amazing.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just invented an elaborate secret society in real time
jokes.punchline: She breaks to admire her own invention, getting distracted by her tangent
jokes.explanation: The self-interruption to compliment her own improv is perfectly Leslie. It shows how her enthusiasm derails even her own sentences. Good economy — this button lands cleanly and doesn't overstay its welcome.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Allison, welcome to the Parks Department. This is where we take taxpayer money and convert it into the slow, painful erosion of individual liberty through burdensome regulations and unnecessary bureaucratic oversight.

dialogue.speaker: Allison
dialogue.line: That's... not really what we do here.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's what government does everywhere. We're just more honest about it.

jokes.text: What brings you to the festering putrid stink hole on the armpit of freedom? That's what he calls city hall.
jokes.setup: Ron addresses Allison at city hall
jokes.punchline: Ron has a pre-existing, elaborate negative epithet for city hall ('festering putrid stink hole on the armpit of freedom'), and the follow-up clarification is unnecessary but perfect
jokes.explanation: The description is gloriously over-the-top while being deeply Ron — he despises government, and his disdain is poetic. 'Stink hole on the armpit of freedom' layers two body-part metaphors for maximum disgust. The matter-of-fact clarification ('That's what he calls city hall') implies this is Ron's standard greeting, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Why don't you shut your mustache?
jokes.setup: Ron suggests Allison get a paying job instead of the government internship
jokes.punchline: Allison fires back with 'Why don't you shut your mustache?' — a nonsensical insult that addresses Ron's most iconic physical feature
jokes.explanation: This is a standout joke. 'Shut your mustache' is grammatically impossible, logically nonsensical, and yet somehow perfectly aimed at Ron Swanson — whose mustache IS his most defining feature, both physically and symbolically. The economy is perfect (four words). The absurdist logic (treating a facial feature like a mouth to be shut) is inspired. Ron's reaction ('Sorry') plays beautifully — even Ron is momentarily disarmed by it. It's a joke that could only work here: the target is specific, the construction is novel, and the payoff is proportionate. Near-perfect joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I should warn you, the sawmill is extremely dangerous. Last year, someone lost a finger.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, it was two fingers. And a toe.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, it was a whole foot. The point is, people are always losing limbs.

jokes.text: Oh, really? Is it worth a few bucks to get a million splinters in your fingers and then cut off your fingers accidentally, 'cause that will happen.
jokes.setup: Allison mentions she needs money for school; Ron is pitching her the sawmill job
jokes.punchline: Ron enthusiastically describes the horrifying physical dangers of the sawmill job as if they're selling points
jokes.explanation: Ron treating accidental amputation as an acceptable workplace footnote ('cause that will happen') is very Ron. His anti-safety, pro-danger philosophy is consistent and the dark casualness lands well.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I did Tim Hautner a favor once.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Built him a whole sawmill.

jokes.text: I have tolerated Leslie's pro-government ways because her annoying kindness and generosity sneakily made me like her as a person. But I draw the line at corrupting America's youth.
jokes.setup: Ron's talking-head about Leslie and the Allison situation
jokes.punchline: Ron's highest compliment for Leslie is that her kindness 'sneakily' got through his defenses — framing genuine affection as a betrayal — then ending on 'corrupting America's youth' for government internships
jokes.explanation: The joke works on an emotional level too — this is a genuine expression of Ron's love for Leslie wrapped in his anti-government philosophy. 'Sneakily made me like her as a person' is both funny and touching. 'Corrupting America's youth' for what is a government internship shows Ron's ideology at its most absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, if you don't help me recruit Allison, I'm going to come to your office every single day and reorganize your filing system alphabetically.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You wouldn't dare.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, I would dare. And then I'd color-code it.

jokes.text: I once did him a favor. I built his sawmill.
jokes.setup: Ron says he knows Tim Hautner from the sawmill and can get Allison a job there
jokes.punchline: The 'favor' turns out to be that Ron personally built the entire sawmill — the most Ron Swanson sentence possible
jokes.explanation: Perfect Ron Swanson economy. The beat is masterful: 'I once did him a favor' sets up an ordinary network connection, then 'I built his sawmill' lands as both a character joke and an absurd escalation. Ron casually built an entire industrial facility as a 'favor.' The pause between the two sentences (implied by the period) is crucial to the joke. This is textbook deadpan understatement — the mundane framing of an extraordinary act. Exceptional character integration because this is genuinely believable for Ron.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Why did you pay for a limo?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's the law. If you're going to prom, you have to arrive in a limo. It's in the Constitution.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's not in the Constitution.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, it should be.

jokes.text: Interns become full-time staff, become department directors. Circle of life. The seasons turn. It's really quite beautiful.
jokes.setup: Leslie's talking head about why she wants Allison as an intern
jokes.punchline: Leslie elevates bureaucratic career advancement to Shakespearean/nature-documentary levels of profundity, ending with 'It's really quite beautiful'
jokes.explanation: Leslie treating government career trajectories like the Lion King is a reliable character comedy well. The escalation to 'Circle of life' and 'The seasons turn' is good, and 'It's really quite beautiful' as a button works. Not her sharpest material but consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Orin?

dialogue.speaker: April's mom
dialogue.line: It's me, April's mom. I've decided to embrace my daughter's goth aesthetic.

jokes.text: And if Ron tries to stop me, he can eat a big ol' bowl of butts.
jokes.setup: Leslie's warm reflection on mentorship suddenly pivots to competitive declaration about Ron
jokes.punchline: 'A big ol' bowl of butts' is a comically mild curse for an otherwise passionate declaration — the juvenile insult undercuts the drama
jokes.explanation: The tonal whiplash from 'circle of life' profundity to 'eat a big ol' bowl of butts' is well-executed. The phrase itself is inventively childish and very quotable. Leslie's competitive friendship with Ron always generates good comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Where's all my equipment? This is ridiculous!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I need a Kanye-themed mountain structure. Like, a 'Dropout' peak with a 'Graduation' summit. It needs to exist and it needs to exist now.

jokes.text: Ben and Andy's pre-prom hype sequence: 'Pawnee! Class of '99! Uh-huh! Ooh!'
jokes.setup: Ben and Andy are getting ready for prom
jokes.punchline: Two grown men in their 30s doing genuine high school prom hype energy — the joke is entirely the visual incongruity of their age and enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: Functional energy-setter for the prom sequence. The humor is in watching 30-something men adopt teenage prom rituals. Not a crafted joke so much as a performance moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I can't believe they're out of elliptical cartridges. Do you know how hard it is to find replacements for my specific model?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I have this whole system. I've got them organized by year, by manufacturer, by resistance level. It's like my vinyl collection.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Speaking of which, I just scored three mint condition original pressings at the record shop. They're absolutely fire, no cap. I'm gonna have to reorganize my whole crates section.

jokes.text: Girl, you look creepy.
jokes.setup: April shows up to prom dressed in a way that apparently looks creepy (likely deliberately so)
jokes.punchline: Andy's frank compliment-as-criticism — delivered with enthusiasm — suggests April looks great by her own standards
jokes.explanation: A quick, efficient character beat. Andy saying 'you look creepy' as an admiring compliment (because for April, creepy IS beautiful) perfectly captures their relationship. Economy is very high — three words say everything about both of them.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Just throw them away, bro. They're just records. It's not like they're important or anything.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Tom, these are first pressings. Original vinyl from the 70s and 80s.

jokes.text: Would you like a drink? All this stuff is free. No, it's not. Why'd you pay for a limo? Because it's prom. If you don't show up in a limo, legally, they can't let you in.
jokes.setup: April notes the limo was an unnecessary expense
jokes.punchline: Andy insists there's a legal requirement to arrive in a limo for prom — stated with complete conviction as if this is well-established law
jokes.explanation: Andy's invented social laws (stated as legal fact) are a recurring character gag. 'Legally, they can't let you in' for a prom limo is a funny application of false authority to a trivial social custom. The confidence of the delivery is what sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I only went to prom for 15 minutes. By the time I finished my grooming routine—exfoliating, moisturizing, cologne application, hair gel, teeth whitening strips—everyone was already slow dancing. I walked in right as they were playing the last song.

jokes.text: I'm April's mom. / You two look adorable. / Ugh, just take the picture already, mom. / My baby is all grown up. / Have her home by 11:00. / Mom, stop embarrassing me.
jokes.setup: Andy and April are taking prom photos with 'Orin' (April's friend who apparently showed up)
jokes.punchline: Andy fully commits to playing April's embarrassing mom for the photos, hitting every mom trope (baby is grown up, home by 11, stop embarrassing me) while April plays along as the exasperated teenager
jokes.explanation: Andy and April role-playing a mom-daughter dynamic for a prom photo is genuinely delightful and reveals why their relationship works — Andy's childlike enthusiasm meets April's sardonic dry wit and they find magic in absurd scenarios. The beats are all classic mom/daughter tropes but executed with enough specificity to land fresh.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, I know I'm late. I was at this thing.

dialogue.speaker: Date
dialogue.line: Tom, you said you'd be here at 8. It's 10:30.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, I'm here now. Can we just dance or whatever?

jokes.text: Where's everything I requested? Where's my smoke machine? Where's my girls dressed in Teddy Bear costumes? Where's my Yeezus Mountain?
jokes.setup: Tom surveys the prom venue and finds it lacking
jokes.punchline: Tom's reasonable requests escalate from smoke machine (somewhat normal) → girls in teddy bear costumes (bizarre) → Yeezus Mountain (completely invented)
jokes.explanation: 'Yeezus Mountain' is the peak of this joke — a completely invented concept that clearly references Kanye West's Yeezus album but has been extrapolated into a physical installation. Tom's entitlement and grandiosity for a free high school prom is consistently funny, and the escalating absurdity of his requests works well.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: An A-plus? That's... that's fine. I mean, it's just a letter. Letters are arbitrary. A, B, C, D, E, F... they're all just shapes that someone decided to use. I could have invented better letters. But whatever, an A-plus is cool I guess.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You've had that framed for three hours.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to frame it differently now.

jokes.text: I specifically requested elliptical cartridges for the turntables. How am I supposed to keep my Husker Du albums in near-mint condish?
jokes.setup: Ben also surveys the DJ setup and finds it lacking
jokes.punchline: Ben's complaint is about maintaining his Husker Du vinyl collection in 'near-mint condish' (abbreviating 'condition' while discussing a niche 80s punk band) — the opposite of DJ Robo Drop's aesthetic
jokes.explanation: Ben being a vinyl-obsessed Husker Du fan (classic nerd/alt-rock taste) juxtaposed with Tom's EDM world is perfectly calibrated character comedy. 'Near-mint condish' is a funny shorthand — he uses casual slang ('condish') for something he's extremely precious about.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I went to prom when I was 12.

jokes.text: Hey, I have an idea. Why don't you throw them in the garbage?
jokes.setup: Ben worries about his Husker Du vinyl
jokes.punchline: Tom's casual suggestion to destroy the irreplaceable albums is delivered as friendly advice
jokes.explanation: Clean quick punch. Tom's contempt for anything pre-digital is consistent, and the economy is good. Not the sharpest joke but earns its keep.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Prom is like... it's like a beautiful butterfly made of music and dreams, you know? And that butterfly is also somehow a sandwich, but like, a really good sandwich that makes you cry happy tears because you realize that time is just a construct and we're all really just dancing skeletons trying to find meaning in the void.

jokes.text: My prom was right after I got impeached, so I couldn't leave the house without being egged. But my parents threw me a prom in our living room. I think I'm still messed up from it.
jokes.setup: Tom shares his prom story
jokes.punchline: Tom matter-of-factly reveals he was impeached (presumably as student body president or similar) before prom, couldn't leave due to egg-throwing, had a house prom, and is 'still messed up from it' — treating a bizarre childhood political scandal as a normal teen hardship
jokes.explanation: The joke works because of what goes unexplained: Tom casually mentions being impeached as a teenager as if it's a normal hardship, moves past it, and the 'living room prom' is its own tragedy. 'I think I'm still messed up from it' applies to the home prom but the audience wonders if the impeachment is the real damage. The restraint in not explaining the impeachment is the right choice.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Prom is like a movie, right? You go in with all these expectations, and then you watch it, and it's amazing.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But then you watch it again, and you're like, 'Wow, that wasn't as good as I remembered.'

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So you keep watching it, thinking maybe you missed something the first time.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: After watching it ten times, I can confirm: it's still bad.

jokes.text: I was actually only at my prom for 15 minutes. By the time I got my Armani suit pressed and got the little dimple on my tie just right, it was 11:45 P.M. My date was pretty pissed, but, uh, I looked fly as hell.
jokes.setup: Tom shares more about his prom experience
jokes.punchline: Tom's consolation for missing most of prom and angering his date is that he 'looked fly as hell' — vanity trumps all relationship concerns
jokes.explanation: The joke is entirely in the ratio: he spent his entire prom prep time and arrived at 11:45 PM, but this is framed as a worthwhile trade because the suit was perfect. The small detail of 'the little dimple on my tie just right' shows Tom's obsessive vanity. 'My date was pretty pissed, but, uh, I looked fly as hell' is excellent structure — the 'uh' pause before the punchline gives it a confessional quality.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Fine, you can dance.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: But I'm going to be checking the bushes for abandoned babies.

jokes.text: Leslie, thanks again. We just wouldn't have had a prom without you. This is A-plus work. A-plus! Thank you, Principal Russell. Can I get that in writing?
jokes.setup: Principal Russell praises Leslie's work organizing prom
jokes.punchline: Leslie's immediate request to have the A-plus put 'in writing' — treating informal praise like an official academic grade she needs documented
jokes.explanation: Leslie's compulsive need to document and legitimize praise is a reliable character trait. The request to have a conversational compliment put in writing is both funny and a little heartbreaking (she needs the validation). Works well.

dialogue.speaker: High schooler
dialogue.line: Your music is so mid and cringe, it's giving major flop energy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, what? Mid? I'm... I'm not sure what that means. Is that bad?

dialogue.speaker: High schooler
dialogue.line: It's giving clueless dad vibes.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay, but specifically, what did I do wrong? I can fix it. I'll add more cowbell or... or less cowbell?

jokes.text: Oh-ho, Leslie. You haven't changed since high school.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks for the A-plus in writing
jokes.punchline: Principal Russell's fond recognition implies this is exactly the behavior Leslie exhibited in high school — confirming she was always this way
jokes.explanation: A functional beat that confirms Leslie's character consistency, but it's not a strong joke on its own — more of a setup for the next beat. The reaction from a principal who apparently knew her does add a layer of world-building.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What does 'no cap' mean?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It means 'no lie.' Kids say it now.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So if I said 'no cap' to someone at work, they'd understand me?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No cap, they would think you're having a stroke.

jokes.text: I can't believe he gave you an A-plus. Oh, did he? I didn't even notice. No bigs.
jokes.setup: Ben teases Leslie about caring about the A-plus
jokes.punchline: Leslie's transparently fake nonchalance — 'I didn't even notice. No bigs.' — while clearly having noticed and cared enormously
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat. 'No bigs' as Leslie's attempt at casual cool is a nice generational language touch. The hypocrisy of pretending not to care while having literally asked for documentation is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay Allison, here's what you're gonna do. You're gonna take this form, fill it out in triplicate, then take it to the Department of Parks assessment office on the third floor.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Actually, the assessment office moved to the basement. You'll need to take the old elevator, not the new one.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, why would you say that? Now she's completely confused!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I was providing accurate information.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes, but you're ruining the fun! See? Everyone's laughing and having a great time, and you just had to be all truthful and helpful about it.

jokes.text: I attended prom with Susan Hofler. Picked her up in my truck, we slow-danced to a Merle Haggard song, and then I left early to go to my shift at the quarry. I was 12 years old. Never went again. Felt like I had outgrown it.
jokes.setup: Ron's talking head about his prom experience
jokes.punchline: 'I was 12 years old.' Delivered as a casual aside — Ron attended prom at age 12, had a quarry shift, and felt he'd outgrown proms. The nonchalance is the joke.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's single best joke, and one of the finest Ron Swanson jokes in the series. The structure is perfect: each sentence builds a picture that seems exaggerated until 'I was 12 years old' reframes everything. The slow-dance at prom (romantic) to immediately leaving for a quarry shift (industrial child labor) is a devastating juxtaposition. 'Felt like I had outgrown it' is the perfect coda — Ron at 12 felt prom was beneath him, which somehow tracks completely. The economy is extraordinary: six sentences establish an entire character mythology. This is among the best examples of deadpan understatement in sitcom writing — comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor, arguably exceeding it in character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I didn't go to my own prom because I was dating Coach K during his championship run. He needed me there every night. It was the right call.

jokes.text: Well, we did it. We went to prom. Yay! Let's go now.
jokes.setup: They've just arrived at prom and the decorations are up
jokes.punchline: April treats the act of arriving as the entirety of the prom experience and immediately proposes leaving
jokes.explanation: The joke works through extreme compression: 'We did it. Yay! Let's go now.' April treats a rite of passage as a checkbox. 'Yay!' delivered with zero enthusiasm is perfect April. The speed of the pivot from 'we're here' to 'let's leave' makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I think Ben and I are fundamentally incompatible. He's organized and optimistic, and I'm just... not.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Girl, you're not incompatible. You're just different. And different is good. My husband and I are nothing alike, but we make it work because we actually love each other.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: But what if the differences are too big?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Then you break up. But you're not even trying. Stop feeling sorry for yourself and actually talk to your man.

jokes.text: Look around. The bloom of youth. Like flowers on the sunset of an eagle's poetry.
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to convince April to enjoy prom
jokes.punchline: Andy's poetic description collapses into incoherence — 'flowers on the sunset of an eagle's poetry' is the attempt of a poetic soul with no poetic vocabulary
jokes.explanation: Andy's pseudo-poetic gibberish is a recurring pleasure in Parks and Rec. 'Flowers on the sunset of an eagle's poetry' achieves the right level of accidentally surreal beauty — each word is individually appropriate to the register he's attempting, but they assemble into nonsense. This could only come from Andy Dwyer. High quotability because it sounds almost profound.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I got Allison a job.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: She starts Monday at the Parks Department.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: If anyone needs to reach me, I'll be on my mobile telephone.

jokes.text: It's like the movie Expendables 2. First time, hated it. Second time, hated it. Third time, it was okay. But then the fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, tenth time I watched it, I realized something. It's just -- it's not good. It's not a good movie.
jokes.setup: Andy tries to convince April to give prom a chance by analogy
jokes.punchline: The analogy builds as if it's leading to a redemption of Expendables 2, but the conclusion after ten viewings is simply 'it's not a good movie' — the commitment to the bit (ten viewings) is both the joke and the character revelation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is impeccable: the analogy promises a redemption arc (first time hated, second time hated, third time okay...), but skips dramatically to 'fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, tenth time' which already tells us Andy rewatched a movie he didn't like ten times — then the conclusion is a resigned acknowledgment that it was never good. The joke works because Andy's enthusiasm for bad movies, his persistence, and his eventual acceptance of mediocrity is deeply funny and perfectly true to character. The escalating viewings (he skips '8th and 9th' implying even more) and the flat delivery of the conclusion make this a standout bit.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Is that a phone from 1987? Ron, did you get that phone from a museum? You're supposed to *look at* the exhibits, not *become* one.

jokes.text: Um, I'm gonna go to the girls' bathroom to check the trash cans for babies.
jokes.setup: Andy asks April to dance with him at prom
jokes.punchline: April's stated reason for not dancing is that she needs to check bathroom trash cans for abandoned babies — this is presented as a completely normal errand
jokes.explanation: An exceptional April line. The joke operates on multiple levels: it's dark (checking for abandoned babies), absurd (treating it as a routine task), and character-specific (April would absolutely do this). The delivery as a casual logistical statement — 'but you can dance if you want' — makes it perfect. It's also weirdly touching that April would actually check, suggesting she cares about babies despite her nihilistic persona. High quotability. This line belongs in an April Ludgate greatest hits.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We weren't harassing Allison, we were just... aggressively encouraging her.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Not a 2 Chainz crowd. I'll throw on some yeezy in a second.' Ben: 'Jeezy? Weezy?'
jokes.setup: Tom tries to read the room musically and names 'Yeezy' (Kanye)
jokes.punchline: Ben doesn't recognize 'Yeezy' and guesses rhyming alternatives — 'Jeezy? Weezy?'
jokes.explanation: Ben's 'Jeezy? Weezy?' is funny because he's rhyming his way through rappers he actually knows, and the options he lands on reveal his knowledge is just barely deeper than zero. Good character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I'll stop bothering you about this. I promise.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But what if we negotiated on just bringing it up to an A-minus?

jokes.text: The stuff you're playing is so old, it's probably trinking on grizzledump.
jokes.setup: A teenager continues to criticize Ben's music
jokes.punchline: The teen uses completely invented slang ('trinking on grizzledump') with perfect confidence, implying either it's too cool for Ben to know or the writers invented it to emphasize how unknowable teen slang is
jokes.explanation: Deliberately invented slang as a comedy device — making 'grizzledump' and 'trinking' sound exactly like teen slang while being completely meaningless. This works because Ben (and the audience) can't tell if these are real words or not, which captures the authentic experience of cultural obsolescence. 'Trinking on grizzledump' has a phonetic rightness that makes it feel real. Highly quotable precisely because it sounds like something that should mean something.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, so Allison, here's what I see in your future. You're going to get promoted to manager within six months. Then you'll move to a bigger city, maybe Chicago or Denver. You'll meet someone wonderful, get married in a small ceremony—very tasteful. Then you'll have two beautiful children. You'll write a book about your experiences in local government that becomes a bestseller. Then you'll run for city council. Then state senate. Then governor. And then, Allison, you're going to run for President of the United States and you're going to win. You'll be the greatest president this country has ever seen. Mount Rushmore will have to add a sixth face just for you.

jokes.text: Hey, what's grizzledump? And why is trinking on it bad?
jokes.setup: The teen uses the invented slang
jokes.punchline: Ben earnestly tries to decode the slang, treating it as a genuine language to be learned — his sincerity about being out of touch is the joke
jokes.explanation: Ben sincerely wanting to know 'why is trinking on it bad?' is great — he's treating made-up nonsense as a real cultural phenomenon he needs to understand. The callback doubles down on the absurdist slang joke and Ben's desperate attempt to remain relevant.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Alright kids, have a great time at prom! Remember to be safe, be respectful, and if you do decide to have sex, make sure you're both on the same page about what that means.

dialogue.speaker: Kid
dialogue.line: Ms. Knope, what does that mean?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, like, some people think sex means just the penetrative kind, but actually there are many forms of sexual expression, and you should explore what feels right for you and your partner. Also, don't forget to use protection, because STDs are very real, and some of them don't have cures, so really think about—

dialogue.speaker: Principal
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's enough.

jokes.text: I don't know what's cool anymore. What's grizzledump, Ben? What's grizzledump?
jokes.setup: Ben has just discovered he doesn't know what 'grizzledump' means
jokes.punchline: Ben's existential crisis about not knowing what's cool, punctuated by repeating 'What's grizzledump?' as if that's the specific knowledge that would restore his sense of identity
jokes.explanation: Ben's generational crisis crystallized into a single absurd word. The repetition of 'What's grizzledump?' — directed at himself — is the right emotional escalation. The joke works because grizzledump isn't real, but Ben's feelings about not knowing it are completely real and relatable.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I mean... snoopies. That's what I call them. You know, like Snoopy? From Peanuts?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's not... I didn't invent that. That's a real thing.

jokes.text: So just pull the rope? That's right.
jokes.setup: Leslie has given an elaborate, detailed tutorial on how to pull the balloon drop rope
jokes.punchline: Allison cuts through Leslie's over-explanation by reducing it to its essential action: 'So just pull the rope?' Leslie confirms with 'That's right.'
jokes.explanation: A clean straight-man moment. Leslie's inability to give simple instructions without elaborate ceremony is a known character trait, and Allison cutting through it efficiently is a good comedic beat. The economy of the exchange (six words total) is high.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: That's a nice dress. Where did you get it?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: A dead woman's closet. She was my size. I waited three days for her to stop needing it.

jokes.text: Watch the cage. / Watch the faces! [repeated alternating commands as Allison stands between them]
jokes.setup: Ron and Leslie are in direct conflict over whether Allison should watch the balloon cage (Ron's craftsmanship) or the faces of the crowd (Leslie's public service ethos)
jokes.punchline: Their philosophical battle has been reduced to competing one-sentence commands barked at a teenager — the absurd smallness of the argument vs. the grandeur of what each side represents
jokes.explanation: The Ron vs. Leslie debate has been perfectly distilled to two competing phrases: 'Watch the cage' (pride in craftsmanship, tangible results) vs. 'Watch the faces' (the human impact of public service). The joke is that both are sincere expressions of each character's worldview, compressed to absurdity. The poor teenager caught between them is a great visual.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm not having fun because I'm thinking about all the pranks I pulled in high school. Like when I convinced everyone that we had a new student named Jorge who didn't exist, and I made a whole Facebook page for him. Or when I told people that Principal Henderson was having an affair with the lunch lady, which he actually was, but nobody believed the rumor until it came out in the newspaper. Or when I systematically convinced my entire grade that Mondays were being moved to Wednesday.

jokes.text: Congratulations, Ron. You've ruined prom. Everybody's having a terrible time.
jokes.setup: Ron and Leslie's argument has apparently caused the balloon drop to go wrong or the mood to be killed
jokes.punchline: Leslie's sarcastic accusation, delivered with full dramatic conviction — but 'everyone's having a terrible time' at a prom where we've seen people enjoying themselves is clearly hyperbolic
jokes.explanation: A functional beat that caps the Ron/Leslie argument, but it's not particularly sharp. Leslie's dramatic declarations work better when the absurdity is more specific.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, I have developed a sophisticated system for tracking your level of craziness. It's based on a logarithmic scale, with data points including the number of binders you've created in a given week, how many times you've said the word 'amazing,' and the circumference of your eyes when you're excited about something.

jokes.text: I didn't go to my prom. I was dating an older fella back then. Like I'm gonna dance with a bunch of kids while he's coaching Duke to the final four.
jokes.setup: Donna shares her prom story in a talking head
jokes.punchline: The 'older fella' turns out to have been coaching Duke basketball to the Final Four — Donna was skipping prom to be with a significant college basketball figure
jokes.explanation: Perfect Donna Meagle. Her romantic history always involves implausibly impressive men, and 'coaching Duke to the Final Four' is both specific and exactly right for her character. The casual 'like I'm gonna dance with a bunch of kids' frames this as an obvious priority — skipping prom for a prestigious basketball coach is, in Donna's world, completely reasonable. The joke lands because it's consistent with years of Donna mythology.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have a system. Every time Leslie does something insane, I make a little note of it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, you keep a crazy log?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm up to 247 entries.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That seems about right.

jokes.text: I just want to go home, but I feel bad because Andy's having such a good time. How can I love someone when I hate everything he loves?
jokes.setup: April's talking head about her prom experience
jokes.punchline: April frames a fundamental romantic incompatibility as a philosophical crisis — loving someone despite hating everything they love — while the show has spent episodes showing why they work
jokes.explanation: More warmly funny than laugh-out-loud, but April's dramatic framing of normal relationship compromise as an existential problem is good character work. 'How can I love someone when I hate everything he loves?' is genuinely quotable despite being (or because it's) slightly earnest.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A level 6 incident? Ron, those uniforms were an absolute travesty! The colors were completely washed out, the fit was unflattering, and don't even get me started on the stitching quality. This isn't just about soccer—this is about civic pride and representing our community with dignity!

jokes.text: That's not true. He loves a lot of dumb stuff, but he loves you the most.
jokes.setup: April questions how she can love Andy when he loves things she hates
jokes.punchline: Donna's advice simultaneously validates April's complaint ('he loves a lot of dumb stuff') and delivers genuine romantic wisdom — the backhanded compliment as relationship counseling
jokes.explanation: Donna delivering relationship wisdom through an insult is a perfect character move. 'He loves a lot of dumb stuff, but he loves you the most' acknowledges Andy's foolishness without undermining the emotional truth. It's simultaneously a roast and a love declaration. The economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You know, Leslie, life is like a construction blueprint. You can plan it out perfectly, but once you start building, things never go according to plan. A pipe bursts. The contractor disappears with your money. Your wife leaves you. And suddenly you're standing in an empty lot wondering where it all went wrong.

jokes.text: Hey, girl. Are you ready to go? I feel like I told you to wait in the car. Yeah. See? Be direct.
jokes.setup: Donna advises April to be direct with Andy; immediately a teen boy speaks to his date
jokes.punchline: The teen's 'I feel like I told you to wait in the car' (extremely direct, also rude) is used by Donna as an example of successful directness — she misses the dysfunction entirely
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed visual joke. Donna says 'be direct,' the universe immediately provides an example of directness that is actually a guy being dismissive to his girlfriend, and Donna takes it as confirmation of her advice. The joke works because 'I feel like I told you to wait in the car' is technically direct communication but socially terrible — and Donna's endorsement of it is inadvertently bad relationship advice. Good structural timing.

jokes.text: First of all, your telephone is ridiculous.
jokes.setup: Ron announces he called Tim Hautner on his 'mobile telephone'
jokes.punchline: Leslie's first counter-argument is about Ron's phone being ridiculous (implying he has an antiquated or bizarre phone, consistent with Ron's technophobia)
jokes.explanation: A visual gag dependent on what Ron's phone looks like. The joke is inferred from context — Ron would have a flip phone or brick phone — and Leslie's first priority being to insult the phone rather than the argument is a good beat. Rewatch bonus for the visual.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I stuffed the ballot box. I wanted to see if I could commit an undetectable crime.

jokes.text: I wouldn't say 'harassing' so much as persistently tormenting.
jokes.setup: Principal Russell accuses both Leslie and Ron of harassing Allison
jokes.punchline: Leslie corrects 'harassing' to 'persistently tormenting' — a word that is objectively worse — as if making a meaningful semantic distinction
jokes.explanation: An excellent irony/semantic comedy joke. Leslie instinctively disputes the word 'harassing' and offers a correction that is demonstrably more severe — 'persistently tormenting.' The humor is that she thinks she's clarifying/defending herself but has actually confessed to something worse. The delivery would be crucial: Leslie genuinely believes this is a meaningful distinction. Very quotable and a clean structure.

jokes.text: No! Don't be disappointed in me. I've never had a principal or a teacher be disappointed in me. I'm not sure that I'm equipped to handle it.
jokes.setup: Principal Russell says he's disappointed in Leslie
jokes.punchline: Leslie's genuine distress at receiving a principal's disappointment for the first time — treating it like a novel trauma she hasn't developed coping mechanisms for
jokes.explanation: This is peak Leslie Knope. Her lifelong academic perfectionism means she has literally never experienced a teacher's disappointment, and she genuinely doesn't know how to process it. 'I'm not sure that I'm equipped to handle it' is both funny and a tiny bit heartbreaking. The character integration is near-perfect — this could only come from Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: This is the best night of my life! I'm at prom! I'm dancing! I'm wearing a tuxedo!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We just got kicked out.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know! Isn't it great? We're rebels now. We're like James Dean. Except cooler because we got kicked out of prom. James Dean never got kicked out of prom because he was too cool to go to prom in the first place!

jokes.text: I think the only thing that matters is whatever A-pluses may or may not have been handed out, you know, are still in effect in perpetuity.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just agreed to stop competing with Ron over Allison; Principal Russell is satisfied
jokes.punchline: Immediately after agreeing to back off, Leslie uses lawyerly language to ensure her A-plus is grandfathered in — she agrees to stop the behavior but not the reward
jokes.explanation: Leslie negotiating the preservation of her A-plus while backing down on the internship battle is perfectly in character. 'In perpetuity' is a funny word for a compliment from a high school principal. Her priorities are exactly backwards and she doesn't notice.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You're having fun now.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, only because we're breaking things and being irresponsible.

jokes.text: Attention, everyone. Now it is time for the most magical moment of any high school prom: The announcement of the winner of the Parks and Recreation's coveted summer internship.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just promised to stop competing for Allison's internship
jokes.punchline: Immediately after her promise to the principal, Leslie gets on the microphone to announce the internship winner — having completely violated her commitment within thirty seconds
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the immediacy of the hypocrisy — she literally just promised to stop, then hijacked the prom PA system. 'The most magical moment of any high school prom' framing a government internship announcement as the climax of prom night is great Leslie delusion.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm worried I'm getting old and out of touch. What if I'm already dressing like an old person and don't even realize it?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I mean, look at me. Sensible shoes, khakis, a button-down shirt...

jokes.text: You're gonna take this internship. You're gonna fall in love with public service. You're gonna rise through the ranks. You'll take over Ron's job as parks director. You'll win a seat in congress, and then you and I will run against each other as president, but right before we find out who won, I'm gonna pat you on the back and say, 'It's your turn, kid.'
jokes.setup: Allison says she hasn't decided about the internship
jokes.punchline: Leslie has planned Allison's entire career trajectory through a presidential race, complete with a scripted gracious concession speech, in real time
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in Leslie Knope character comedy. The escalation is perfect: internship → full-time staff → department director → parks director → congress → presidential race → gracious concession speech she's already scripted. The final line — 'It's your turn, kid' — delivered as a pre-written speech she's already composed for a future moment that hasn't happened is exactly who Leslie is. The joke also carries emotional weight about Leslie potentially leaving Pawnee. Strong rewatch bonus.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You know what I've noticed? Every billionaire has a weird haircut. Like, they all have that one weird thing with their hair. Elon Musk has that thing, Jeff Bezos is bald, Bill Gates has that cut...

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's because they stop caring about their appearance once they have enough money.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I think it's the opposite. I think the weird haircut is what makes them a billionaire. Like, they're so focused on their vision that they just let their hair do whatever it wants, and that confidence and that weirdness is what gets them to a billion dollars.

jokes.text: Sorry, children. Forget this happened. Continue with your awkward close-quarters gyrating.
jokes.setup: Leslie's announcement has fallen flat; she retreats
jokes.punchline: 'Awkward close-quarters gyrating' as Leslie's clinical description of slow dancing — she can't even apologize without editorializing
jokes.explanation: 'Awkward close-quarters gyrating' is a genuinely funny euphemism for slow dancing. The word 'gyrating' is doing heavy lifting — it's technically accurate but sounds clinical and slightly horrifying. Leslie's inability to let any moment pass without commentary is well-deployed here.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You'll never be as old as me.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's true.

jokes.text: And if this is the evening you decide to have sex, use protection, please!
jokes.setup: Leslie is wrapping up her PA address to the teen prom
jokes.punchline: Leslie cannot help herself — she adds mandatory safe sex advice to the prom PA announcement, treating it as a public service obligation
jokes.explanation: Perfect Leslie. She cannot disengage from her civic duty — even after the internship disaster, she uses the remaining PA time to deliver sex ed. The 'please!' at the end is a great touch — she's politely requesting safe sex. The character integration is near-perfect; no other character on this show would end a prom address this way.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm going to mentor you so hard. I'm going to mentor you every single day. I'm going to mentor you so much you're going to get sick of mentoring.

dialogue.speaker: Allison
dialogue.line: Please don't.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Too late. It's happening. You're going to be the most mentored person in the entire state of Indiana.

jokes.text: Go ahead. Play whatever you want. Can't be any worse than this.
jokes.setup: Ben offers to take over DJ duties
jokes.punchline: Tom's defeated permission — 'can't be any worse than this' — is a concession that marks his existential music collapse
jokes.explanation: A functional beat setting up Ben's musical redemption. Tom's defeated acceptance is slightly funny but not especially crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Allison
dialogue.line: Everyone, I'd like you to meet my boyfriend.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait... Jeremy Jamm?

jokes.text: Hey, I love this song! / You actually like this? / Yeah, dude, it's classic rock.
jokes.setup: Ben puts on a song and a teenager reacts
jokes.punchline: The teenager loves the song Ben put on — the same teenager who didn't know Ja Rule — showing that Ben's 'old' music is now 'classic rock' to the next generation
jokes.explanation: The generational joke completes its arc: Ben's music has gone from embarrassingly old to 'classic rock.' The subversion is clean — his cultural obsolescence has paradoxically given him credibility with a different generational framework. Good callback payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, you're dating Greg Pikitis? Greg Pikitis is the worst. He's a punk, he's a delinquent, he spray-painted my house!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But you know what? You seem like a smart, capable woman, and if you think Greg Pikitis is worth your time, then... he's probably not that bad. Greg seems great.

jokes.text: Well, there's more where that came from, snoopies! Sorry. Tried to use slang. That just came out.
jokes.setup: Ben is energized by the teenager's positive response
jokes.punchline: Ben attempts to use youth slang and says 'snoopies' — an invented/wrong term — then immediately self-corrects with 'Sorry. Tried to use slang. That just came out.'
jokes.explanation: Ben's instinct to use slang while being incapable of it — 'snoopies' as the word that just 'comes out' — is beautifully specific. The immediate self-awareness and apology ('Sorry. Tried to use slang. That just came out.') is the right button. Ben's self-consciousness is endearing and the specific failure ('snoopies') is funnier than any generic bad slang would be.

jokes.text: I only listen to CDs. It's the way music like this was meant to be heard. But it's not even auto-tuned.
jokes.setup: Ben and the teenager bond over music
jokes.punchline: Ben's audiophile CD defense is met with a teenager baffled by the absence of auto-tune — two completely different music value systems making no sense to each other
jokes.explanation: The generational divide made concrete through format and production values. 'But it's not even auto-tuned' as a criticism of classic rock is a good joke — the teenager considers the absence of auto-tune a flaw rather than a feature. The parallel snobberies are funny.

jokes.text: Where'd you get that dress? I was buried in it.
jokes.setup: A teenager compliments/questions April's unusual prom dress
jokes.punchline: April claims she was buried in the dress — implying she was buried alive, or that it's a burial garment, or that it was exhumed
jokes.explanation: This is possibly the single best line in the episode. The economy is perfect — four words. The misdirection is elegant: 'Where'd you get that dress?' expects a store name or designer, and 'I was buried in it' is the maximum possible subversion of that expectation. The ambiguity is deliberate and perfect — was she the one buried? Was she burying someone? Is this a funeral dress? All readings are funnier than the last. The character integration is flawless because this is exactly the answer April Ludgate would give and no other character on television would say this. It's also a complete conversation-stopper, which is itself funny. One of the finest examples of economy and misdirection in the series.

jokes.text: Babe, huge news. I just got us invited to Damian Keating's barn party. He's captain of the soccer team, and he has a fake I.D., so I think he can get us all free beer.
jokes.setup: Andy is excited about a social opportunity at prom
jokes.punchline: Andy — a 33-year-old married man — is thrilled to have been invited to a high school kid's barn party and references the kid's fake ID as a pathway to free beer
jokes.explanation: Andy's complete lack of adult self-awareness — getting genuinely excited about high school social hierarchy and a teenager's fake ID — is deeply funny and perfectly in character. He's treating the invitation to a barn party like a diplomatic breakthrough.

jokes.text: I spent four years making fun of everyone and hiding mops so the janitor would think he was going insane.
jokes.setup: April reflects on her high school experience while lamenting she and Andy would never have dated
jokes.punchline: Her summary of four years of high school: mockery + a sustained psychological torment campaign against a janitor
jokes.explanation: The mop-hiding detail is the heart of this joke. April summarizes her high school years and the specific detail she includes is a years-long psychological gaslighting campaign against a janitor using stolen mops. 'So the janitor would think he was going insane' shows deliberate, patient malice that is both horrifying and funny. The commitment required — hiding mops for four years — implies this was a sustained project. Perfectly April and highly quotable.

jokes.text: We got that limo for three more hours. I think the extra length could help us get us over that lake.
jokes.setup: April suggests they bail and use the limo
jokes.punchline: Andy suggests using the limo's length to jump the lake that his car couldn't clear — a callback to 'laked' and a completely insane escalation
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback. Andy suggesting the limousine's extra length could help clear the lake he failed to jump earlier demonstrates that he still thinks the lake-jumping was a viable plan that simply needed better equipment. The callback rewards attention and deepens the original joke. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: I have never told you this, but I actually have a ten-point scale for how insane you are being. I observe your behavior, and if it's a five or below, I say nothing.
jokes.setup: Ben's talking head about managing Leslie
jokes.punchline: Ben has a secret formalized metric for monitoring Leslie's behavior level — treating his wife's actions as data to be scored
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. The joke is that Ben has formalized his husband role into a monitoring system, complete with intervention thresholds. The reveal that he says nothing for a 5-or-below implies he regularly observes insane behavior and consciously decides not to engage. This speaks volumes about their relationship in the funniest possible way. The clinical language ('I observe your behavior') applied to his wife makes it funnier.

jokes.text: If it reaches a six, like for example the incident with the girls' soccer uniforms back in '05...
jokes.setup: Ben describes his Leslie behavior scale
jokes.punchline: Ben references 'the incident with the girls' soccer uniforms back in '05' — a mysterious event he knows in detail despite having only met Leslie years later (or maybe he's aware of her legendary local history)
jokes.explanation: The specificity of '05 and 'girls' soccer uniforms' creates a mystery that the show doesn't solve — which is the right choice. The implication that Leslie's past madness is documented and referenced by her husband is funny. The callback setup for the next beat.

jokes.text: A seven is when I lock you in your office until you cool down. This Allison Gliffert thing may have hit an eight. I have the police on standby.
jokes.setup: Ben explains his Leslie behavior scale with escalating intervention levels
jokes.punchline: Level 7 is office lockdown; level 8 has police on standby — Ben has actual law enforcement contingency plans for his wife's behavior
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'I say nothing' (level 5 or below) to 'I lock you in your office' (level 7) to 'I have the police on standby' (level 8) is brilliantly calibrated. Each level reveals more about the extremity of Leslie's behavior history. Ben has actual, pre-arranged police contingency plans for his wife's enthusiasm. The word 'standby' implies a direct line. This is a great escalation joke and an excellent callback payoff.

jokes.text: Blueprints for the future are a fool's errand. They're like blueprints for a house. Nice to have, but any foreman with half a brain doesn't need to look at them.
jokes.setup: Leslie shares her concerns about leaving Pawnee and securing the future
