jokes.punchline: Ron's metaphor for why future blueprints are useless is... blueprints for a house. He uses the word 'blueprint' literally and then undermines the very trade (architecture/construction) he respects
jokes.explanation: The joke has two layers: Ron says 'blueprints for the future are a fool's errand, they're like blueprints for a house' — the comparison is circular (he compares metaphorical blueprints to literal blueprints). Then he adds that a foreman with half a brain doesn't need to look at them, which is both Ron's philosophy and a dismissal of the safety and precision that makes construction work. The self-undermining logic is perfectly Ron.

jokes.text: I just wish once you would say something stupid so I could ignore it.
jokes.setup: Ron has given Leslie genuinely wise, thoughtful advice about enjoying the present
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response to good advice is frustration that she can't dismiss it — her affectionate exasperation with Ron's wisdom
jokes.explanation: Excellent line. The joke is that Leslie is explicitly wishing Ron were stupider so she could maintain her stubbornness. 'So I could ignore it' is the perfect button — she's not saying she disagrees, she's saying she wants permission to not be moved by it. The economy is near-perfect and it's genuinely touching as well as funny. A great Ron-Leslie relationship joke.

jokes.text: I broke the box, and I threw away all the votes, and I voted for you a thousand times.
jokes.setup: The prom king/queen vote has been announced and Andy Dwyer has won
jokes.punchline: Andy cheerfully confesses to destroying the ballot box, discarding all legitimate votes, and stuffing the ballot himself a thousand times — with zero guilt
jokes.explanation: The joke escalates: 'I broke the box AND threw away all the votes AND voted for you a thousand times' — each confession is worse than the last. Andy's guileless delivery ('I voted for you a thousand times' as a romantic gesture) is perfect. He's committed massive electoral fraud as an act of love and sees nothing wrong with it. Very Andy.

jokes.text: Hi, Pawnee High. As your prom king, I'm your ruler. Silence!
jokes.setup: Andy takes the microphone as prom king
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately declares himself 'ruler' and commands silence — treating prom king as actual political sovereignty
jokes.explanation: Andy's immediate power trip as prom king is funny and in character. 'Silence!' as a royal decree at a high school dance is a good escalation. The gap between prom king and 'ruler' is the joke.

jokes.text: My first decree of power is to declare that the prom queen shall be my wife, April Ludgate, who is the best thing that's ever happened to me who came to prom even though she hates it.
jokes.setup: Andy uses his 'ruler' powers to declare a prom queen
jokes.punchline: His royal decree includes 'who came to prom even though she hates it' as part of the official royal proclamation — turning a private accommodation into a public honor
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the specific inclusion: Andy's 'best thing that's ever happened to me' and 'who came to prom even though she hates it' being delivered as a royal proclamation is both funny and genuinely sweet. The comedy comes from Andy's inability to separate the ceremonial from the personal — he broadcasts April's discomfort as a badge of honor.

jokes.text: Andy's prom king speech about April: 'My first decree of power is to declare that the prom queen shall be my wife, April Ludgate, who is the best thing that's ever happened to me who came to prom even though she hates it.'
jokes.setup: Andy uses his prom king powers to name his prom queen
jokes.punchline: 'Who came to prom even though she hates it' — the qualification undermines the grandeur while being genuinely sweet
jokes.explanation: Andy's speech is both sweet and funny. The 'decree of power' language (callbacks his ruler declaration) and the honest qualification 'even though she hates it' make this a character-perfect moment. Not the sharpest joke but landing in a warm place.

jokes.text: Give me this. Always next year. No, there isn't. I'm a senior.
jokes.setup: Andy takes a crown/scepter from a teenager at the prom
jokes.punchline: Andy's consolation ('always next year') is deflated by the teenager pointing out she's a senior — there is no next year
jokes.explanation: A quick deflation joke. Andy's casual disregard for the fact that this is the teenager's one prom is funny and slightly cruel. The exchange is economical and lands.

jokes.text: This is your wife? How old are you? He's 33, and I'm 47/immortal. Get out.
jokes.setup: A student/chaperone realizes April and Andy are married adults at prom
jokes.punchline: April's age response — '47/immortal' — followed immediately by 'Get out' from whoever is expelling them
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. '47/immortal' is an inspired April answer — she gives a specific age (47, which is wrong but sounds deliberate) combined with 'immortal' as if she has two age systems. The slash construction implies both are simultaneously true. It's absurdist, dark, and perfectly April. The immediacy of 'Get out' as the response makes it even better — her answer is so strange it accelerates their eviction. The joke earns every point.

jokes.text: High school forever!
jokes.setup: Andy and April are being kicked out of prom
jokes.punchline: Andy's exit declaration is 'High school forever!' — a rallying cry that is both sad (he's 33 and being ejected from a high school prom) and triumphant in Andy's mind
jokes.explanation: A quick button. 'High school forever!' as a departing cry from a 33-year-old being kicked out of prom is both pathetic and triumphant, which is Andy's entire emotional register.

jokes.text: Yeah, you're having fun now. I rigged an election and got kicked out of prom. I can get on board with that.
jokes.setup: April's talking head about the night's events
jokes.punchline: April's concession that she 'can get on board' with an evening of election rigging and prom ejection — this qualifies as a good time by April's standards
jokes.explanation: The capsule summary of April's ideal evening: election fraud + ejection from a venue. This is also a callback/payoff to the entire Andy-April prom arc — she came reluctantly and found her way to enjoying it through chaos. Perfect character button.

jokes.text: My life is over. I'm officially old and uncool. Might as well start wearing a plaid shirt and a tie and khakis and whatever shoes you're wearing.
jokes.setup: Ben's talking head after his DJ failures
jokes.punchline: Ben's description of total stylistic defeat is directed at the interviewer — 'whatever shoes you're wearing' implies the camera operator has terrible shoes, completing Ben's self-roast
jokes.explanation: A good meta-mockumentary beat where Ben addresses the interviewer/camera. 'Whatever shoes you're wearing' is a nice aside that creates a visual joke without showing the shoes. The self-deprecating description of uncool clothing is well-observed.

jokes.text: Richard Branson and Mark Cuban are too busy making deals to keep up with what the kids are into. How else do you explain their terrible haircuts?
jokes.setup: Tom tries to console Ben by saying he's too busy for youth culture
jokes.punchline: Tom explains Branson and Cuban's bad haircuts through the same logic — billionaires are too busy for grooming — which is absurd but internally consistent with Tom's world view
jokes.explanation: Tom comparing Ben to Branson and Cuban as a compliment, then landing on 'terrible haircuts' as the shared trait, is a good comedic turn. The logic is absurd (billionaires' hair explained by business focus) but Tom delivers it with such confidence it works. A nice consolation joke.

jokes.text: And, hey, you may be old, but you'll never be as old as me. Yeah. You're old as shit.
jokes.setup: Tom continues consoling Ben about being old and uncool
jokes.punchline: Tom offers the backhanded comfort that Ben will never be as old as Tom, then Ben agrees enthusiastically — 'You're old as shit' — turning the attempted consolation into a mutual roast
jokes.explanation: A quick friendship beat. The reversal where Ben agrees a bit too enthusiastically is a decent button. Not exceptional but functional.

jokes.text: Greg Pikitis. What up, Knope?
jokes.setup: Allison says she wants to introduce Leslie and Ron to her boyfriend; Leslie and Ron have just decided she's wonderful
jokes.punchline: The boyfriend is Greg Pikitis — Leslie's recurring teenage nemesis from earlier seasons — who greets her with casual disrespect ('What up, Knope?')
jokes.explanation: This is a perfect sitcom callback structure and a great cold-water ending to the Allison subplot. Just when Leslie (and the audience) has decided Allison is wonderful, the reveal of Pikitis as her boyfriend recontextualizes everything. 'What up, Knope?' delivered with casual teenage disrespect is the right tone — it's not dramatic, it's just Pikitis being Pikitis. The setup is earned through the entire episode's investment in Allison's promise. Strong rewatch bonus for longtime Parks fans who remember Pikitis.

jokes.text: You might say that.
jokes.setup: Allison asks 'You guys know each other?' seeing Leslie's reaction to Pikitis
jokes.punchline: Leslie's loaded understatement — 'You might say that' — implies a history so fraught it defies simple description
jokes.explanation: A clean understatement button. The restraint of 'You might say that' when Leslie clearly wants to say much more is good comedy of suppression.

jokes.text: Ron, upon learning Allison is Pikitis's girlfriend: 'Offer is off the table. She's a terrible person with terrible judgment.'
jokes.setup: Ron and Leslie both discover Allison is dating Pikitis
jokes.punchline: Ron — who spent the entire episode competing against Leslie for Allison's loyalty — immediately withdraws his offer based solely on her boyfriend choice
jokes.explanation: The callback lands perfectly. Ron spent the entire episode fighting Leslie for Allison's professional future; the Pikitis reveal is enough for him to abandon his position entirely and agree with Leslie's implicit judgment. 'Terrible judgment' about a person's boyfriend is Ron's version of a deep insult. The episode-long competition resolves in two sentences.

jokes.text: Offer is off the table. She's a terrible person with terrible judgment.
jokes.setup: Allison and Pikitis walk away together
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately reverses her entire mentorship investment and character assessment of Allison because her boyfriend is Pikitis — the speed of the reversal is the joke
jokes.explanation: The entire episode's B-plot collapses in one sentence. Leslie's confidence in Allison's 'presidential potential' becomes 'terrible person with terrible judgment' in the span of discovering her boyfriend. The absoluteness of the reversal is very Leslie — and also correctly identifies Pikitis as a red flag. The joke also works as a dark commentary on how quickly we reverse our assessments.

jokes.text: Pikitis!
jokes.setup: Ron sees Greg Pikitis
jokes.punchline: Ron recognizes Pikitis and bellows his name — Ron apparently also has a history with Pikitis, confirming he is universally known as a menace
jokes.explanation: The final punchline of the episode. Ron's single-word exclamation — 'Pikitis!' — implies his own history with the kid while also serving as a perfect button. The economy is absolute: one word does everything. For Parks fans who know Pikitis, this lands as a great callback. Even for new viewers, the sheer conviction of Ron's reaction communicates everything needed.

tmdb_overview: In the midst of flu season, a sick Leslie and Andy struggle to book performers for the Unity Concert. Meanwhile, Tom heads to a wine competition in search of a sommelier for his new restaurant, and Ben seeks drunken help from Ron with a personal problem.
insight: High-density character comedy sustains 86-point score across 71 jokes in prom setting.
